The .map() method in JavaScript is used to create a new array by applying a function to every element of an existing array. It does not change the original array; instead, it returns a transformed version of it.

1. Basic Syntax

const newArray = oldArray.map((element, index, array) => {
  // Return the new value for the new array
});
  • element: The current item being processed.
  • index: (Optional) The index of the current item.
  • array: (Optional) The original array being mapped.

2. Simple Example: Doubling Numbers

Let's take an array of numbers and create a new array where every number is doubled.

const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

const doubled = numbers.map(num => num * 2);

console.log(doubled); // Output: [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
console.log(numbers); // Output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (Original remains unchanged)

3. Example: Extracting Data from Objects

This is one of the most common real-world uses for .map()—extracting a specific property from an array of objects.

const users = [
  { id: 1, name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com" },
  { id: 2, name: "Bob", email: "bob@example.com" },
  { id: 3, name: "Charlie", email: "charlie@example.com" }
];
